subject: barcodes
title: Cracking the Code on a Cereal Box
summary: How 95 thin stripes encode 12 digits, read fine upside down, and catch their own mistakes.

keys.prompt: How can a scanner read a UPC upside down without getting the digits backward?
keys.answer: Left-side digits have an odd number of black modules and right-side digits an even number. That parity tells the scanner which way it's reading.

keys.prompt: What does the UPC check digit do?
keys.answer: It's computed from the other 11 digits (odd positions × 3, plus even positions, rounded up to a multiple of 10). If any one digit is misread, the math fails.

keys.prompt: Why did IBM's straight-line code beat RCA's bull's-eye?
keys.answer: The bull's-eye circles tended to smear when printed. Laurer's lines didn't smudge, fit on small packages, and a laser could read them from any direction.

cards.title: The engineer who said no
cards.text: In the early 1970s, RCA owned the patent on a round bull's-eye barcode, and IBM engineer George Laurer's manager wanted him to stick with the bull's-eye. He refused, and pitched straight lines instead. "My nature and my training would not allow me to support something I didn't believe in," he said. His design is the one on nearly everything you buy.

cards.question: A UPC ends with a check digit. If the scanner misreads exactly one digit, how often do you think the check digit catches it?
cards.reveal: Every time. A UPC catches 100% of single-digit errors (it's swapped neighbors that slip past about 11% of the time).

cards.title: Stripes are bits
cards.text: A UPC-A is 95 modules wide, where a module is the thinnest possible stripe. Each of its 12 digits takes exactly 7 modules: two bars and two spaces, each 1 to 4 modules wide. The other 11 modules are guard patterns at the start, middle and end that help the scanner lock on. Count the black bars and you get 30.
cards.example: In bar code language, a 1 on the left side is space-space-bar-bar-space-space-bar: 0011001.

cards.title: Upside down? No problem
cards.text: Each left-side digit has an odd number of black modules (odd parity); each right-side digit has an even number. Right-side digits are also the optical inverse of left-side ones: bars become spaces. So after the start or end guard, the scanner checks the parity and knows which direction it's reading.

why.q: Why would a supermarket barcode need to work in both directions?
why.a: Cashiers swipe items at every angle. The code had to be read from any direction and at speed, so the symbol itself tells the scanner its orientation.

cards.title: The self-checking digit
cards.text: The last digit is a check digit. Add the digits in odd positions and multiply by 3. Add the digits in even positions. The check digit is whatever brings that total up to a multiple of 10. Change any one digit and the total no longer works, so the scanner rejects the read.
cards.example: For 03600029145: odd positions 0+6+0+2+1+5 = 14, × 3 = 42. Even positions 3+0+0+9+4 = 16. 42 + 16 = 58, so the check digit is 2.

why.q: Why multiply some positions by 3 instead of just adding every digit?
why.a: Plain adding can't notice two neighbors swapped, since the sum stays the same. Weighting alternate digits by 3 catches most swaps too.

cards.title: Lines beat circles
cards.text: Joe Woodland's patented bull's-eye could be read from any angle, but RCA's printed circles tended to smear. Laurer's straight bars didn't smudge and a laser could scan them from any direction. The first real UPC scan came on June 26, 1974, in Troy, Ohio: a pack of Juicy Fruit gum, 67 cents.
cards.example: Woodland got the original idea from Morse code, dragging his fingers through beach sand to make wide and narrow lines.

cards.title: Every version gets its own number
cards.text: After the first digit, five digits name the manufacturer and five name the product. Every variation counts as a different product. GS1 US, which hands out these numbers, sells a single one for $30, or a block of 10 for $250 plus $50 a year.
cards.example: Say you start a T-shirt brand with 3 sizes and 3 colors. That's 3 × 3 = 9 products, so you need 9 barcodes.

examples_by_interest.golf: Say you sell golf balls in 4 colors, in sleeves of 3 or boxes of 12. That's 4 × 2 = 8 products, so you need 8 barcodes.
examples_by_interest.business: Say your candle shop sells 5 scents in 2 sizes. That's 5 × 2 = 10 products, so a block of 10 numbers for $250 covers you exactly.

cards.question: Laurer refused to back a design he thought would fail, even though his boss wanted it and RCA already owned the bull's-eye patent. When is it smart to push back like that, and when is it just being stubborn?
nudges: What evidence did he have that circles would smear?
What would he need to show his bosses to win?

questions.q: A real UPC starts 04210000526. Its odd-position digits add to 13 and its even-position digits add to 7. What's the check digit?

options.why: Yes: 13 × 3 = 39, plus 7 is 46, and 4 more makes 50.
That's what you'd get if you skipped the × 3 step: 13 + 7 = 20. Multiply the odd sum by 3 first.
6 is the last digit of 46. The check digit is what you add to reach the next multiple of 10.
Close. Try 13 × 3 + 7, then count up to the next multiple of 10.

questions.q: How does the scanner know a UPC is upside down?

options.text: Left digits have odd parity and right digits have even parity
options.why: Right. Whichever parity it sees first tells it the direction.

options.text: The numbers printed underneath are upside down
options.why: The scanner reads the bars, not the printed numbers.

options.text: It can't, so cashiers must hold items right side up
options.why: UPCs were designed to be read from any direction.

options.text: The check digit always comes first
options.why: The check digit is always the last digit, on the right side.

questions.q: Your bakery sells cookies in 4 flavors and 3 box sizes. How many barcodes do you need?

options.why: Yes. Each flavor-and-size combo is its own product: 4 × 3 = 12.
That's 4 + 3. But every combination needs its own number, so multiply.
One number per product type isn't enough. Each version gets its own.
That counts flavors but not sizes.

sources.title: Universal Product Code
sources.supports: UPC-A is 95 modules: 12 digits of 7 modules each (two bars and two spaces, 1–4 modules wide) plus 11 guard modules; 30 bars; left digits odd parity, right digits even parity, right digits the optical inverse, letting the scanner read in either direction; number system digit, 5-digit manufacturer code, 5-digit product code, check digit; the check-digit method and the 03600029145 → 2 example; the real code 042100005264 (check digit 4); 100% of single-digit errors and about 89% of transpositions detected; first scan of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit at Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio on June 26, 1974, 67 cents.

sources.title: The UPC
sources.supports: RCA owned the bull's-eye patent and it was prone to smearing when printed; Laurer refused his manager's appeal to stick with the bull's-eye, with the quoted line; his linear code wouldn't smudge, could be scanned omnidirectionally with a laser, and fit on most products; Woodland's beach-sand idea from Morse code.

sources.title: How to Get a UPC Barcode
sources.supports: 3 sizes × 3 colors = 9 barcodes for a T-shirt; a single GS1 US GTIN costs $30 with no renewal fee; 10 numbers cost $250 initially plus $50 a year.
